entries.title: Choron and Foyot
entries.summary: Two daughters of béarnaise, each made by one addition. Choron folds in tomato cooked down to a thick paste, coral and tangy; Foyot whisks in glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, tawny and deeper. Brennan's serves both.
entries.guest: Both are béarnaise, the warm tarragon butter sauce. Choron adds tomato, tangy and herbal, on our Eggs Sardou; Foyot adds a reduced beef glaze, richer, with the Chateaubriand.

paras: Choron and Foyot are two daughters of béarnaise, the warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter built on a sharp reduction of vinegar, shallot and tarragon. An emulsion is fat held as tiny droplets in a little water, here by the yolk. Each daughter is one addition to a finished béarnaise. Choron folds in tomato cooked down to a thick paste, which turns the sauce coral, a soft orange pink, and adds a gentle sweetness and tang under the herbs.

Foyot whisks in glace de viande, brown stock boiled down until thick and syrupy, which turns the sauce tawny and gives it a deep, savoury, meaty taste. Both are on the Brennan's menu: learn the parent, then the one addition.

Start from a sound béarnaise: about 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz) of butter gives roughly 300 ml (1 1/4 cups) of sauce. For Choron, fold in 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) of tomato reduced to a paste, about one part to six of sauce. For Foyot, whisk in 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) of warm, melted glace de viande, a spoonful at a time, because glace is strong and often salty; season only at the end.

Make the tomato first. Cook chopped ripe tomatoes, or good tinned purée, in a wide pan over moderate heat, stirring often, until the water has gone and a spoon drawn through leaves a clear line; pass it through a fine sieve and let it cool to warm. Tomato paste cooked for a minute in a dry pan does the same job. Make the béarnaise, then fold the warm tomato through it off the heat. Escoffier's Choron leaves out the final chopped tarragon and chervil; many kitchens keep them.

For Foyot, melt the glace without boiling it and whisk it into the finished béarnaise a spoonful at a time, tasting as you go. Hold both like béarnaise: warm, around 60°C (140°F), in a bain-marie, a pan of warm water, never on direct heat, and made in small batches through service.

Wet tomato is the classic fault, and the reason the tomato is reduced. Fresh tomato is mostly water, and a sauce of yolk and butter has little water to spare: watery purée makes Choron thin and slack, and if the balance tips far enough it splits into a greasy pool. Tomato cold from the fridge can break it too, and raw tomato leaves a sharp, metallic edge that cooking down softens.

Foyot fails differently: too much glace makes it salty, heavy and muddy, and cold glace sets in streaks before it blends. A split sauce of either kind is mended like any béarnaise, whisked drop by drop into a little warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl.

Choron is named for Alexandre Étienne Choron, chef de cuisine at the Voisin restaurant in Paris, remembered for the Christmas menu he served there in 1870, during the Siege of Paris, when the cut-off city ate whatever it could find. Whether he created the sauce or it was named in his honour is not recorded, so tell it as tradition.

Foyot takes its name from the Restaurant Foyot in Paris, on the rue de Tournon facing the Senate. Many texts call the same sauce Valois; others treat the two as separate sauces and disagree on what divides them, so teach both names.

At Brennan's, Choron replaces the usual hollandaise on the Eggs Sardou, over poached eggs, crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach; the house words for it are tangy and herbal. Foyot comes with the Roasted Chateaubriand, the centre of the beef tenderloin roasted whole for two. Tenderloin is lean and mild, so a rich, savoury sauce brings the depth the meat lacks.

Say sho-ROHN and fwah-YO, the weight on the last syllable of each. To a guest, Choron is béarnaise with tomato, tangy and herbal; Foyot is béarnaise made richer with a reduced beef glaze. Both are made with egg yolk and butter, so any question about eggs or dairy goes to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Demi-glace
entries.summary: Espagnole and brown stock simmered together and reduced by half until glossy: the working mother of the classical brown sauces. Bordelaise, Robert, chasseur, madère and périgueux start from it, and many modern kitchens make it from reduced brown stock alone.
entries.guest: Demi-glace is a deep, glossy brown sauce made by slowly reducing roasted veal or beef stock. It is the base of the classic French steak sauces.

paras: Demi-glace means half glaze: a brown sauce reduced halfway towards glace, the thick, syrupy glaze that sets hard when cold. Classically it is espagnole, the roux-thickened brown sauce, simmered with an equal amount of brown stock and reduced by half, then skimmed, strained and often finished with Madeira or dry sherry. Brown stock is made from roasted bones and vegetables, so demi-glace tastes of roasting: deep, meaty and rounded, with body from the roux and from the gelatin of the bones.

It matters because it is the working mother of the brown family. Espagnole is rarely served as it is; demi-glace is what the saucier, the cook in charge of sauces, reaches for to start a bordelaise, a Robert or a chasseur.

Classical demi-glace is equal parts espagnole and brown stock, reduced by half: 1 litre (about 1 quart) of each, simmered down to about 1 litre (about 1 quart), then finished off the heat with about 100 ml (about 7 tbsp) of Madeira or dry sherry. For the modern version, roughly 4 litres (about 1 gallon) of brown stock reduces to 1 litre (about 1 quart).

Bring the espagnole and stock to a simmer in a heavy pan set slightly off centre on the heat, so the liquid rolls up on one side only. Fat and scum gather on the quiet side, where they are skimmed away: the French call this dépouiller. Reduce slowly, skimming every 10 to 15 minutes, until it has lost about half its volume and coats a spoon, two to three hours for a large batch. Pass it through a chinois, a fine conical sieve, lined with muslin for the finest result. Add the wine off the heat, because boiling drives off its perfume.

Many modern kitchens skip espagnole and reduce good brown stock alone the same way. Without roux it is lighter and clearer, its body all gelatin, though it costs more bones and turns sticky if pushed too far. The cues are the same: glossy, nappe (coating a spoon so a finger leaves a clean line), a clean meaty taste, no raw flour, no beads of fat. Cool it from 57°C (135°F) to 21°C (70°F) within two hours and to 5°C (41°F) within six hours in all, as the FDA Food Code sets out.

Demi-glace is the parent the brown daughters share. Bordelaise adds a red wine and shallot reduction and beef marrow; Robert, onion, white wine and mustard; chasseur, the hunter's sauce, mushrooms, shallot, white wine, tomato and tarragon. Madère is demi-glace finished with Madeira, and périgueux adds truffle to madère. The pattern is an aromatic, an acid reduction, the demi-glace and a finish. Reduced further still, brown stock becomes glace de viande.

A gluey, pasty demi-glace had too much roux or was reduced too far: loosen it with brown stock. Bitterness comes from scorching, bones roasted black or a sauce caught on the pan, and cannot be taken out, so the batch is remade. Saltiness comes from salted stock, because reduction concentrates every grain; stock meant for demi-glace is never salted. A greasy surface means poor skimming, and a dull, cloudy sauce was boiled hard.

Bought bases run from frozen, kitchen-quality demi-glace to powders and pastes, and a professional kitchen judges them on the label and in the pan. Stock, or bones and vegetables, should come first, not salt, starch or sugar. Reconstitute it and taste it plain beside the house stock: it should taste of roasted meat, not salt or caramel colouring, and set to a jelly when chilled, the sign of real gelatin. Starch-thickened bases turn pasty when reduced, so test one in a pan sauce before it reaches the line.

Guests rarely meet demi-glace by name; they meet its daughters. Describe it plainly: a deep, glossy brown sauce made by slowly reducing roasted veal or beef stock, the base of the classic French steak sauces. At Brennan's the brown side of the tree shows in the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen; how the kitchen builds that sauce is a question for the chef before you describe it.

cards.front: How is demi-glace reduced, and how long does a large batch take?

cards.front: Why is stock meant for demi-glace never salted?

questions.answer: By reducing brown stock until glossy

questions.q: Why is the stock for demi-glace left unsalted?

questions.q: A demi-glace tastes bitter from scorching. What is the right move?

questions.why: Burnt flavours spread through the whole sauce and no straining or seasoning removes them, so the batch is started again.

questions.q: When does the Madeira go into a classical demi-glace?
questions.answer: Off the heat, at the end
distractors: With the bones, at the start
Into the roux, before the stock
questions.why: Added at the end and off the heat, the wine keeps its perfume; boiled, its aroma is driven off.

questions.q: Reading the label of a bought demi-glace base, what should come first?
questions.why: Ingredients are listed by weight, so a base worth buying leads with stock or bones; one led by salt, starch or sugar tastes of them and turns pasty when reduced.

questions.q: Hot demi-glace must reach 21°C (70°F) within how long?
questions.why: The FDA Food Code has hot food cooled to 21°C (70°F) within two hours and to 5°C (41°F) within six hours in all.

entries.title: Bordelaise, French and New Orleans
entries.summary: Two sauces share the name. French bordelaise is red wine, shallot and herbs reduced into demi-glace and finished with beef marrow; New Orleans bordelaise is a garlic butter with parsley. Knowing which is on the plate changes the wine and the promise.
entries.guest: Here bordelaise can mean two sauces: the French red wine sauce for steak, or the New Orleans garlic and parsley butter. I'll confirm which is on your plate tonight.

paras: Bordelaise, in the Bordeaux style, names two different sauces. French bordelaise is a brown sauce: red wine reduced with shallot, thyme, bay and pepper, simmered with demi-glace, strained, and finished with poached diced beef marrow and parsley. Marrow is the soft fat inside a beef leg bone; poached gently, it melts on the tongue. The sauce is dark, glossy and winey, the steakhouse classic with a porterhouse or an entrecôte, a rib steak.

New Orleans bordelaise is something else: butter, often with olive oil, warmed with plenty of garlic and parsley, sometimes shallot or green onion, and spooned over fish, oysters, pasta or bread. It is pale, fragrant and buttery, with no red wine at all.

For about 500 ml (2 cups) of French bordelaise: 250 ml (1 cup) of red wine with 2 chopped shallots, a sprig of thyme, half a bay leaf and crushed pepper, reduced by three quarters; then 500 ml (2 cups) of demi-glace; then about 100 g (3 1/2 oz) of diced marrow. For New Orleans bordelaise, use 225 g (8 oz) of butter, or butter and olive oil, to 4 to 6 cloves of garlic and a handful of chopped parsley.

French method. Sweat the shallot in a little butter, add the wine, thyme, bay and pepper, and boil until a quarter is left; reduced wine tastes rounder and less sharp. Add the demi-glace and simmer gently, skimming, for 20 to 30 minutes, until it coats a spoon, then strain it through a chinois. Soak the marrow in cold water, dice it and poach it for a minute or two in salted water just below a simmer; boiling would melt it away. Add it at the last moment with the parsley, and a piece of cold butter for gloss.

New Orleans method. Warm the butter and oil over low heat, add finely chopped garlic and cook it gently until soft and fragrant but not brown, then add parsley, salt and pepper; some cooks add lemon or a splash of white wine. Make it close to service, because garlic and parsley fade when held.

The name is for Bordeaux and its red wine. Escoffier's Guide gives bordelaise with red wine, the standard today; a white wine bordelaise is said to be the older, and Escoffier also recorded a white wine version under the name Bonnefoy. Bordeaux cooking uses à la bordelaise for other dishes too: cèpes à la bordelaise are mushrooms sautéed in oil with shallot, parsley and often garlic. How New Orleans came to use the word for a garlic butter is not settled, so give no origin story at the table.

French bordelaise turns thin and sour when the wine is not reduced enough before the demi-glace goes in. Boiled marrow melts into grease; poach it gently and add it last. A gluey sauce had a heavy demi-glace, and brown stock loosens it. New Orleans bordelaise turns bitter and acrid when the garlic browns, so start it in barely warm fat. Held too long, the parsley turns khaki and the garlic flat.

On the Brennan's breakfast and lunch menu, the Pecan Gulf Fish, today's Gulf fish topped with lump crab over cauliflower purée and collard greens, carries a pecan bordelaise. The house reading is that it most likely belongs to the New Orleans family, a butter sauce with toasted pecans worked in. That is a reading, not a recipe: confirm at lineup whether tonight's is garlic butter or red wine based, because it decides the wine. The house pour is the Gainey Chardonnay; if the sauce is red wine based, the Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir takes its place.

The difference matters at the table: a red wine and marrow sauce wants a red with some structure, and a garlic butter on fish wants a white. Never promise red wine or marrow until the kitchen confirms which bordelaise it is. To a guest: French bordelaise is a rich red wine sauce for steak; New Orleans bordelaise is a garlic and parsley butter. Questions about what is in the sauce go to the kitchen.

cards.front: What two sauces share the name bordelaise?
cards.back: The French red wine sauce with demi-glace and beef marrow, and the New Orleans garlic and parsley butter.

cards.front: How is French bordelaise built?
cards.back: Red wine, shallot, thyme, bay and pepper reduced by three quarters, demi-glace added and simmered, strained, then poached marrow and parsley.

cards.front: Why is the marrow poached gently and added last?
cards.back: Boiling melts marrow into grease; poached just below a simmer and added at the end, it stays in soft, rich pieces.

cards.front: What goes into New Orleans bordelaise?
cards.back: Butter, often with olive oil, plenty of garlic and parsley, sometimes shallot or green onion, and no red wine.

cards.front: How is the garlic cooked for New Orleans bordelaise?
cards.back: Gently, in warm fat over low heat, until soft and fragrant; garlic that browns turns the sauce bitter.

cards.front: Where does bordelaise take its name from?
cards.back: From Bordeaux, the city and wine region of south-west France, and its red wine.

cards.front: Under what name did Escoffier record a white wine bordelaise?
cards.back: Bonnefoy. Red wine bordelaise is the standard today, and a white wine version is said to be the older.

cards.front: Why must a server know which bordelaise is on a dish?
cards.back: A red wine and marrow sauce calls for a red; a garlic butter on fish calls for a white. The sauce changes the bottle.

cards.front: Which bordelaise is on the Pecan Gulf Fish?
cards.back: Most likely the New Orleans garlic butter family, with toasted pecans, but it is confirmed at lineup before any wine is paired.

cards.front: What is the steakhouse classic with French bordelaise?
cards.back: A porterhouse or an entrecôte, a rib steak, with the red wine and marrow sauce spooned over.

questions.q: In New Orleans restaurants, bordelaise usually means which sauce?
distractors: A red wine sauce with marrow
questions.why: The city uses the word for butter, often with olive oil, garlic and parsley; the red wine and marrow sauce is the French bordelaise.

questions.q: What goes in last to finish a French bordelaise?
questions.why: After the wine reduction and demi-glace, French bordelaise is finished with gently poached marrow and chopped parsley.

questions.q: Why is the bone marrow for bordelaise never boiled?
questions.why: Marrow is almost all fat, so boiling melts it away; poached below a simmer and added last, it keeps its soft pieces.

questions.q: What happens when the garlic browns in a New Orleans bordelaise?
distractors: The garlic turns sweet and mild
questions.why: Browned garlic turns acrid, so it is cooked gently in barely warm fat until soft and fragrant, never coloured.

questions.q: What is the steakhouse classic served with French bordelaise?
distractors: Roast leg of lamb, studded with garlic
questions.why: The red wine and marrow sauce is made for grilled beef: a porterhouse, or an entrecôte, a rib steak, with the sauce spooned over.

questions.q: Bordelaise is named for which place?
questions.why: Bordelaise means in the Bordeaux style, after the city and its red wine; béarnaise is the sauce named for Béarn.

questions.q: What should a server do before pairing wine with the Pecan Gulf Fish?
distractors: Assume it is the red wine sauce
Pour a Pinot Noir without asking
Treat it as a beurre blanc and pour white
questions.why: The house reads it as the New Orleans butter family but asks servers to confirm, because a red wine sauce changes the pour.

questions.q: Under which name did Escoffier record a white wine bordelaise?
questions.why: Bonnefoy is the white wine bordelaise; Bercy is a shallot and white wine fish sauce, Foyot a béarnaise and marchand de vin a red wine sauce.

entries.title: The béchamel family
entries.summary: The small sauces built on béchamel: Mornay with cheese, Soubise with onion, Nantua with crayfish, crème with cream and cardinal with lobster butter. Each is béchamel plus one defining addition, and the cousins run from macaroni cheese to Oysters Bienville.
entries.guest: These are creamy white sauces built on béchamel, milk thickened with butter and flour. Mornay adds cheese, Soubise sweet onion and Nantua crayfish, classics for gratins and fish.

paras: The béchamel family is every sauce made by adding one thing to béchamel, the white sauce of milk thickened with a white roux, flour cooked in butter without colour. Béchamel is mild by design, which is why it takes additions so well: cheese, onion, cream, a crayfish or lobster butter. Learn the addition and the name tells you the sauce's colour, its taste and what it goes with.

Mornay is béchamel with grated Gruyère and Parmesan melted in off the heat, finished with a little butter and sometimes an egg yolk, which helps it set and brown. It is the sauce of gratins and of glazing, browning a sauce under a hot grill; for fish, classical kitchens add some fish fumet, a concentrated fish stock. Soubise is béchamel with a purée of onions cooked slowly in butter until soft and sweet but never coloured. The older Soubise was onion cooked with rice and puréed; both are ivory, mild and sweet.

Nantua is béchamel with cream and crayfish butter, butter pounded with crayfish shells and strained, garnished with crayfish tails: pink and rich, named for Nantua, a town in the Ain known for its crayfish. It is the classic sauce for quenelles de brochet, poached dumplings of pike, a dish of Lyon. Crème is béchamel reduced with cream and finished with more cream and lemon. Cardinal is béchamel with fish fumet, finished with lobster butter and a pinch of cayenne: coral red.

Make a medium béchamel and cook it out for at least 15 to 20 minutes so no taste of raw flour remains. For Mornay, take the pan off the heat before the cheese goes in, because boiled cheese turns stringy and oily; stir it in a handful at a time, then the butter. For Soubise, sweat sliced onions in butter under a lid, with a splash of water if they threaten to colour, until completely soft, 30 to 40 minutes, then stir them into the béchamel and blend it smooth. For Nantua and cardinal, reduce the béchamel with cream or fumet, then whisk in the crayfish or lobster butter off the heat.

For Mornay, a common working ratio is 1 litre (about 1 quart) of medium béchamel to 100 to 125 g (about 4 oz) of grated cheese, half Gruyère and half Parmesan, and 50 g (2 oz) of butter. For Soubise, about 500 g (1 lb) of onions to 500 ml (2 cups) of béchamel. For crème, reduce 1 litre (about 1 quart) of béchamel with 250 ml (1 cup) of cream, then finish with more cream and lemon.

A grainy or stringy Mornay was boiled after the cheese went in, or made with pre-grated cheese coated in starch: grate it fresh and add it off the heat. An oily Mornay had too much cheese or heat; whisk in a little hot milk. A beige Soubise had its onions coloured, and the only fix is to start them again, low and covered. A gratin that will not brown needs a yolk or more cheese in the sauce and a hotter grill. A Nantua or cardinal that separates had its crayfish or lobster butter added too hot: whisk in a spoonful of hot cream off the heat.

The cheese sauce of the American kitchen, Cheddar melted into béchamel for macaroni cheese, is Mornay's later cousin, and so is the bistro's mustard sauce, béchamel sharpened with Dijon for ham or fish. The croque-monsieur, a toasted ham and Gruyère sandwich, is the everyday Mornay: many cafés top it with Mornay or béchamel and grill it until bubbling, and the croque-madame adds a fried egg.

New Orleans has its own cousin in the sauce of Oysters Bienville: a rich cream sauce with shrimp, mushroom and sherry, baked over oysters on the half shell and gratinéed, browned under heat with a crust of breadcrumbs or cheese.

To a guest, each is a creamy white sauce, and the addition describes it: Mornay is a cheese sauce, Soubise a sweet onion cream, Nantua a crayfish cream. A dish au gratin or Mornay has a browned cheese crust over a creamy sauce. Any question about dairy, gluten or shellfish in these sauces goes to the service note and the kitchen.

ratios.label: Mornay: cheese to béchamel
ratios.value: 100 to 125 g (about 4 oz) of Gruyère and Parmesan to 1 litre (about 1 quart)

ratios.label: Soubise: onions to béchamel
ratios.value: About 500 g (1 lb) of onions to 500 ml (2 cups)

ratios.label: Crème: cream to béchamel
ratios.value: 250 ml (1 cup) reduced into 1 litre (about 1 quart), then more cream and lemon

faults.cause: Boiled after the cheese went in, or pre-grated cheese coated in starch.
faults.fix: Add freshly grated cheese off the heat, a handful at a time.

faults.cause: Too much cheese, or too much heat.
faults.fix: Whisk in a little hot milk or béchamel off the heat.

faults.cause: The onions were allowed to colour.
faults.fix: Start the onions again, low, covered and with a splash of water.

faults.fault: A gratin that will not brown
faults.cause: Too little cheese or no yolk in the sauce, or a grill not hot enough.
faults.fix: Add a yolk or more cheese to the sauce and use a hotter grill.

faults.cause: The crayfish or lobster butter went in over too much heat.
faults.fix: Off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of hot cream.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907), Project Gutenberg eBook 71395

cards.front: How is every sauce in the béchamel family made?
cards.back: Béchamel plus one defining addition: cheese for Mornay, onion for Soubise, crayfish butter for Nantua, cream and lemon for crème.

cards.front: What is sauce Mornay made of?
cards.back: Béchamel with Gruyère and Parmesan melted in off the heat, finished with butter and sometimes a yolk, for gratins and glazing.

cards.front: Why does the cheese go into a Mornay off the heat?
cards.back: Cheese boiled in a sauce turns stringy and oily; melted gently off the heat, it stays smooth.

cards.front: Why add an egg yolk to a Mornay meant for glazing?
cards.back: The yolk helps the sauce set and brown evenly under a hot grill.

cards.front: What is sauce Soubise made of?
cards.back: Béchamel with a purée of onions cooked soft in butter without colour; the older Soubise was onion cooked with rice.

cards.front: What is sauce Nantua, and which dish is it known for?
cards.back: Béchamel with cream and crayfish butter, garnished with crayfish tails: the sauce of quenelles de brochet, poached pike dumplings.

cards.front: How do sauce crème and sauce cardinal differ?
cards.back: Crème is béchamel finished with cream and lemon; cardinal adds fish fumet, lobster butter and cayenne, and is coral red.

cards.front: Why does a Soubise turn beige, and what fixes it?
cards.back: The onions coloured; start them again, low, covered and with a splash of water, so they soften without browning.

cards.front: Which later cousins of Mornay belong to the bistro and the American kitchen?
cards.back: The Cheddar cheese sauce of macaroni cheese, and the bistro's mustard sauce, béchamel sharpened with Dijon.

cards.front: Why is the croque-monsieur called the everyday Mornay?
cards.back: The ham and Gruyère sandwich is often topped with Mornay or béchamel and grilled; a croque-madame adds a fried egg.

cards.front: What is the New Orleans cousin of the béchamel family?
cards.back: The sauce of Oysters Bienville: a cream sauce with shrimp, mushroom and sherry, baked over oysters and gratinéed.

questions.q: What turns a béchamel into Mornay?
questions.why: Mornay is the cheese daughter; crayfish butter makes Nantua, onion makes Soubise and lobster butter makes cardinal.

questions.q: Why is the cheese added to a Mornay off the heat?
questions.answer: Boiling makes it stringy and oily
distractors: It stops the roux from browning
It keeps the sauce from thickening
questions.why: Boiled cheese tightens and lets go of its fat, so it is melted gently into the hot sauce off the heat.

questions.q: Which sauce is béchamel with a purée of soft, uncoloured onions?
questions.why: Soubise is the onion daughter, ivory and sweet; the older version cooked the onions with rice before puréeing them.

questions.q: Which classic dish is served with sauce Nantua?
questions.why: Poached pike dumplings in a crayfish cream are the classic pairing, from Lyon; Nantua is named for a town known for crayfish.

questions.q: What gives sauce cardinal its colour and finish?
questions.why: Cardinal is béchamel with fish fumet, finished with lobster butter for its coral colour and cayenne for a little heat.

questions.q: Why might a cook add an egg yolk to a Mornay for a gratin?
questions.answer: It helps the sauce set and brown
distractors: It keeps the cheese from melting
It stops the milk from boiling
questions.why: A yolk enriches the sauce and helps it set and colour evenly under a hot grill, which is the point of glazing.

questions.q: What does a croque-madame add to a croque-monsieur?
questions.why: The croque-monsieur is ham and Gruyère, often under Mornay; the croque-madame is the same sandwich crowned with a fried egg.

questions.q: The sauce on Oysters Bienville is a cousin of which mother sauce?
questions.why: It is a cream sauce with shrimp, mushroom and sherry, baked and gratinéed, so it belongs with the béchamel family.

questions.q: A Soubise has come out beige. What went wrong?
questions.answer: The onions were allowed to colour
distractors: The cheese went in too late
The roux was cooked too briefly
questions.why: Soubise should be ivory, so the onions are sweated low and covered until soft; browned onions tint the sauce and cannot be undone.
